content: Estrogen vaginal products carry significant risks and should be used with caution. Prolonged use of estrogen increases the likelihood of developing endometrial cancer, which is cancer of the uterine lining. If you have not undergone a hysterectomy (surgical removal of the uterus), your doctor may prescribe a progestin to be used alongside vaginal estrogen. This combination may reduce the risk of endometrial cancer but could increase the risk of other health issues, such as breast cancer. Before starting vaginal estrogen, inform your doctor if you have a history of cancer or if you experience unusual vaginal bleeding. If you notice abnormal or unexpected vaginal bleeding during treatment, contact your doctor immediately. Your doctor will monitor you closely to ensure you do not develop endometrial cancer during or after treatment. Studies have shown that women who take oral estrogen combined with progestins have a higher risk of heart attacks, strokes, blood clots in the lungs or legs, breast cancer, and dementia. Women using vaginal estrogen, either alone or with progestins, may also face an increased risk of these conditions. Inform your doctor if you smoke, have had a heart attack or stroke in the past year, or if you or your family members have a history of blood clots or breast cancer. Additionally, let your doctor know if you have or have had high blood pressure, high cholesterol or fat levels, diabetes, heart disease, lupus, breast lumps, or abnormal mammograms. Be vigilant for symptoms that may indicate serious health conditions, such as sudden severe headaches, vomiting, speech problems, dizziness, fainting, vision changes, chest pain, coughing up blood, shortness of breath, memory or cognitive difficulties, breast lumps, nipple discharge, or leg pain and swelling. If you experience any of these symptoms, contact your doctor immediately. To minimize risks, do not use vaginal estrogen, with or without progestins, to prevent heart disease, heart attacks, strokes, or dementia. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary to manage your symptoms. Regularly consult your doctor every 3–6 months to evaluate whether you should continue, reduce, or stop the medication. Perform monthly breast self-exams and schedule annual mammograms and breast exams with your doctor to detect breast cancer early. Your doctor may recommend more frequent exams based on your medical history. If you are scheduled for surgery or will be on bed rest, inform your doctor. You may need to stop using vaginal estrogen 4–6 weeks before surgery or bed rest to reduce the risk of blood clots. Discuss the risks and benefits of vaginal estrogen with your doctor regularly. Vaginal estrogen is prescribed to treat symptoms such as vaginal dryness, itching, burning, painful or difficult urination, and sudden urgency to urinate in postmenopausal women. Certain brands, like Femring®, are also used to treat hot flashes, while Premarin® cream is used for conditions like kraurosis vulvae, which causes vaginal dryness and discomfort. Vaginal estrogen products come in various forms, including flexible rings, tablets, and creams. Rings are typically inserted into the vagina and left in place for three months, after which they are replaced if treatment is still needed. Tablets are usually inserted daily for the first two weeks, then twice weekly as needed. Creams are applied daily for 2–4 weeks, then reduced to 1–3 times per week or according to a rotating schedule. Always use vaginal estrogen at the same time each day and follow your doctor’s instructions carefully. Do not use more or less than prescribed. To insert a vaginal ring, wash and dry your hands, remove the ring from its pouch, and choose a comfortable position (e.g., standing with one leg raised, squatting, or lying down). Squeeze the ring between your thumb and index finger, press the sides together, and insert it as far back into your vagina as possible. If the ring falls out, wash it with warm water and reinsert it. If it is lost, insert a new ring and leave it in place for up to three months. Contact your doctor if the ring falls out frequently. The ring can remain in place during sexual activity, but if removed, wash it and reinsert it promptly. To use vaginal tablets, tear off one applicator, remove it from its packaging, and choose a comfortable position. Insert the applicator into your vagina as far as comfortable, then press the plunger until you hear a click. Dispose of the applicator after use; do not reuse it. To use vaginal cream, attach the applicator to the cream tube, squeeze the tube to fill the applicator to the prescribed dose, and insert the applicator into your vagina. Press the plunger to release the cream, then remove and clean the applicator with mild soap and warm water. Do not use hot water or boil the applicator. Before using vaginal estrogen, inform your doctor if you are allergic to any ingredients, are taking other medications (including herbal products like St. John’s Wort), or have a history of conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, asthma, migraines, seizures, porphyria, or thyroid, liver, kidney, gallbladder, or pancreatic disease. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, notify your doctor immediately. Some estrogen creams may weaken latex or rubber birth control devices, so discuss alternative contraception methods with your doctor. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while using this medication unless your doctor advises otherwise. If you miss a dose, apply or insert it as soon as you remember, but skip it if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not double the dose to make up for a missed one. Vaginal estrogen may cause side effects, including breast pain, upset stomach, dizziness, mood changes, hair loss, unwanted hair growth, skin discoloration, hot flashes, leg cramps, vaginal irritation, or flu-like symptoms. Severe side effects, such as bulging eyes, yellowing of the skin or eyes, joint pain, rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing, require immediate medical attention. Estrogen use may increase the risk of ovarian cancer or gallbladder disease and may affect growth in children. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Store vaginal estrogen in its original container, tightly closed, at room temperature, away from heat and moisture. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Keep all medical appointments and inform laboratory personnel that you are using vaginal estrogen. Do not share this medication with others, and consult your pharmacist for any questions about refills.
